newsitem.title: VENEZUELA: Venezuela CVG sale fits "bicycle" sell-off theory.
newsitem.headline: Venezuela CVG sale fits "bicycle" sell-off theory.

text.p: The long awaited $3 billion sale of Venezuela's state-owned iron and aluminum firm follows the "bicycle" theory of privatization, analysts said Monday: slow down too much and you fall off -- the crux is to keep going.

With presidential elections scheduled for December 1998, "the privatization has to happen this year, or at the latest early next year, if it's to go ahead at all," said Santander regional analyst Jose Corral.

The sale of a 70 percent share in the companies, currently in the hands of state holding company Corporacion Venezolana de Guayana (CVG), is seen as a high-profile test of Venezuela's economic reform spirit -- both by investors and government.

"When these companies are privatized, privileges and subsidies will be removed, workers moved, strategies changed. We'll be doing at a micro-level what has to be done throughout the whole country," Alberto Poletto, president of Venezuela's Investment Fund, the state body in charge of privatization, said in a recent newspaper interview.
"If we don't manage to transfer the companies to the private sector, international opinion is going to have wider doubts about Venezuela's (economic) reforms," said Poletto.
Theoretically, Venezuela should have no trouble selling its aluminum companies, the largest of the two privatizations.
"The potential is huge," said Credit Lyonnais metals analyst Harald Liberge.

Blessed with abundant bauxite ore and bountiful supplies of cheap, hydro-electric electricity -- a key cost in aluminum production, "Venezuela could become one of the largest and lowest cost aluminum producers in the world," said Liberge.
Venezuela's CVG is the sixth largest single producer in the world, producing around 620,000 metric tonnes per year,
The slated sale date to a short-list of thirteen international heavyweights, which include Alcoa, Reynolds Metals and RTZ Corp, is still the second half of the year.
But if history is any guide, the sale has every chance of being delayed: serious discussion first began in 1989, under former president Carlos Andres Perez's administration.
"You can't really expect them to be sold quickly," said Santander's Corral. "They're complicated companies in bad shape."
But even as the clock ticks, a number of crucial issues remain unresolved -- not least Congress's support.

Last week, opposition party Radical Cause, which along with leading opposition party Democratic Action has strong roots in the CVG's unions, filed for a delay in the privatization so "Congress could have more time to study the process."

Concessions terms for the bauxite mines and CVG's port, Puerto Ordaz, on the Orinoco river, remain unresolved. Treatment of the aluminum companies' $1.2 billion in debt and steel maker Sidor's $600 million in debt is still unclear.
And there is the persistently niggling issue of how to best persuade a consortium of Japanese investors to give up their 20 percent veto share in aluminum smelter Venalum.

Despite repeated attempts, Venezuela has not yet been able to strike a deal with the consortium that includes Showa Denko KK, Kobe Steel Ltd, Sumitomo Chemical Co Ltd, Mitsubishi Materials Corp, Mitsubishi Aluminum Co Ltd and Marubeni Corp.

The Japanese group's intransigence would not halt the sale, but would force the government to accept a lower price, as any new buyer would have to contend with the veto power of an already-entrenched group, analysts said.
"On the other hand, the final buyer will probably get better terms from the Japanese than the Venezuelans ever could," said one investment banker close to the deal.
Time is also limiting for the potential investor. The buyer will want to catch a rising world market currently operating at 92 percent capacity, according to industry analysts.
Finally, and perhaps most importantly, secure handling of the CVG's crippling environmental liabilities, estimated at upwards of $200 million, is a pressing point.
"How the liabilities are handled, who will be responsible and when, is still being discussed," said the investment banker.
"The precise final terms will make the sale go, or not go," he added.
((-- Caracas newsroom, 582 505 2600))
